summary: The IAB's recommended policy on distributing Internet identifier assignment, and on dropping the connected status requirement. It is informational and not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
This memo is advice from the IAB to the Federal Networking Council, and it is addressed to the Federal Networking Council, which sat above the Internet community and funded the American backbones.

Its two asks are administrative. Hand out numbers through more than one registry, and stop deciding who gets into the DNS on the basis of a government approval that was meant for a small research network in the 1970s.

subtitle: The IAB's advice to spread out the handing-out of network numbers and to stop tying registration to "connected" status.

tldr.problem: Network numbers were handed out by one registry in the United States, and only networks that a government sponsor approved could be listed in the DNS. As the Internet grew worldwide, both rules became hard to justify.
tldr.mechanism: The memo makes two recommendations to the Federal Networking Council: delegate blocks of numbers to regional registries, and replace the connected status flag with a published statement of each network's acceptable use policy.
tldr.outcome: It also says that naming and routing should be decoupled, so any registered network can be entered into the DNS. It is an Informational document and says it does not specify a standard.

today: RFC 1174 is an Informational document from August 1990 and has not been obsoleted. It states the official view of the Internet Activities Board at the time, and says that it does not specify a standard.

sections.title: The Two Recommendations and the Number Assignment Plan
sections.content:
This informational RFC represents the official view of the Internet Activities Board and contains two recommendations to the Federal Networking Council. The first is a recommended policy on distributing Internet identifier assignment, that is, a suggestion to distribute the function of assigning network and autonomous system numbers. The second is a recommended policy change to the Internet connected status, that is, a suggestion to drop the notion of connected status in favour of recording the acceptable use policy and traffic access policy for each network, including the explicit suggestion that any registered network may be entered into the DNS database without regard to connected status.

Throughout its entire history the Internet system has employed a central Internet Assigned Numbers Authority for the allocation and assignment of the various numeric identifiers needed for its operation. The IANA function is performed by USC Information Sciences Institute. The IANA has the discretionary authority to delegate portions of this responsibility and, with respect to numeric network and autonomous system identifiers, has lodged this responsibility with an Internet Registry. This function is performed by SRI International at its Network Information Center, the DDN-NIC.

With the rapid escalation of the number of networks in the Internet and its concurrent internationalization, it is timely to consider further delegation of assignment and registration authority on an international basis. It is also essential to take into consideration that such identifiers, particularly network identifiers of class A and B type, will become an increasingly scarce commodity whose allocation must be handled with thoughtful care.

The proposed method of operation is to retain the centralized IANA and IR functions. The IR would continue to be the principal registry for all network and autonomous system numbers and would continue to maintain the list of root Domain Name System servers and a database of registered nets and autonomous systems. In addition, however, the IR would allocate to organizations approved by the Coordinating Committee for Intercontinental Research Networking blocks of network and autonomous system numbers, as needed, and delegate to them further assignment authority. It is recommended that, at least initially, the IR serve as the default registry in cases where no delegated registration authority has been identified.

Copies of the aggregate Internet registration databases should be maintained by the IR and copies provided to each delegated registry, to improve redundancy and access to the information, although updates would still be centralized at the IR, with complete copies redistributed by file transfer or other means on a timely basis. Candidate delegated registries should meet with the IANA and the IR to review operational procedures and requirements and produce documentation to be issued as RFCs. It is recommended that host Domain Name registration continue in its present form, which already accommodates distribution of that function.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the centre, but let it hand out blocks rather than individual numbers, and let regional bodies do the day-to-day allocation. Meanwhile the DNS should be open to everyone with a registered number.

sections.title: The Three Actions on Connected Status
sections.content: The recommendation is a change in the current policy for associating connected status to a subset of networks which have been assigned an Internet identifier. Three actions are recommended. First, the Internet Registry should be instructed to drop all reference to connected status in its databases and in its forms for Internet network and autonomous system registration. Second, the Internet Registry should be instructed to request brief statements of acceptable network usage, access and transit policy for external traffic, that is, traffic entering from or exiting to other networks, from each applicant for a network or autonomous system identifier. Some networks conform to the National Science Foundation acceptable use guidelines; other networks will carry any traffic, for example common carriers; others may prohibit transit use. Retrospective statements should be gathered by the IR for networks already registered, and such statements should be made available on-line and widely publicized. Third, the Internet Registry should be instructed to allow any registered networks to be entered into the Domain Name Server database without regard to connected status.
sections.plainLanguage: Replace the yes-or-no flag with a short published sentence about what each network accepts, and stop letting the flag decide who appears in the DNS.

sections.title: Why Connected Status Had to Go
sections.content:
With the demise of the ARPANET and the growth of a global Internet, the administration and registration of Internet network numbers had outgrown its initially conceived client base of military, government and government-sponsored research organizations. Since the international growth extended the Internet community to industry and a broad range of academic and research institutions, some of the criteria for assignment and use of Internet network numbers had to be re-evaluated.

In the early phases of the Internet research project, numbers were assigned only to networks of organizations participating in the research effort. Later, other organizations with networks were assigned numbers and allowed to interconnect if they were parts of the United States Government or sponsored by a Government organization. To ensure global uniqueness, a single Internet Registry was designated, the Defense Data Net Network Information Center at SRI International. As the Internet protocols became popular in the commercial marketplace, many organizations purchased and installed private networks that needed network number assignments but were not intended to be connected to the federally-sponsored system. The IR adopted a policy of assigning network numbers to all who requested them, while distinguishing networks permitted to link to the global Internet by assigning them connected status. Essentially, this meant that the network to which the number was assigned had the sanction of a United States Government sponsoring organization to link to the Internet.

The present day Internet encompasses networks that serve as intermediaries to access the federally-sponsored backbones. Many were initiated under the sponsorship of the National Science Foundation, and some were founded without federal assistance as consortia of using organizations. The Government has expressed a desire that all such networks be self-supporting. To achieve that, the intermediate networks had to support an increasingly varied range of users. In essence, each network needs to be able to determine, on the basis of its own criteria, with which networks it will interconnect and for which networks it will support transit service. There is no longer a simple binary correlation between connected status and acceptable use policy.

The matter becomes even more complex with the large and growing number of non-United States networks joining the global Internet. It is inappropriate to require that all of these networks adhere to United States access and use criteria; rather, it can only be required that the traffic they send through the federally-sponsored networks be consistent with the federal criteria.

Since the concept of a single, global connected status is no longer meaningful, it is recommended that it be retired and that new characteristics be defined that networks could use to determine a specific network's eligibility to communicate with others. Some attributes that might be useful to track, and could be used as criteria to determine the acceptability of Internet traffic for routing purposes, include country codes and conformance to acceptable use policy for NSFNET, MILNET, NSI, ESnet, NORDUnet and similar networks. The IR would update the Internet-Number-Template to query applicants for the necessary information, collected in a database containing, for instance, a matrix of network numbers over policies, though the policies might be presented in narrative form. The usage policies of the various networks must be publicly available.

Under this proposal the IR would be charged with the registration and administration of the Internet number space but not with the enforcement of policy. It should collect enough information to permit network administrators to make intelligent decisions about the acceptability of traffic destined to or from each legitimate Internet number. At a later step it is anticipated that it will be desirable to distribute the IR function among multiple centers, for example with centers on different continents, which should be straightforward once the IR function is divorced from policy enforcement.
sections.plainLanguage: The flag was a leftover from a small research network run on government money. By 1990 the Internet included commercial carriers and networks outside the United States, and a single yes-or-no answer from Washington no longer described them.

sections.title: Policy-Based Routing and the Limits of the Idea
sections.content:
It is already true in the current Internet that there are restrictions on certain traffic on particular networks. Two intermediate level networks that are willing to carry arbitrary traffic can link with each other but are barred from passing commercial traffic, or any other traffic that is not for academic or scholarly purposes, across the federally-sponsored backbones.

Routing of traffic based upon acceptable-use policies requires a technical ability known as policy-based routing. At the present time the mechanism available in the Internet operates at the level of an entire network: all users and hosts on a network are subject to the same routes for a given destination. Using this mechanism, a network maintains routes and provides transit services only for networks with compatible use policies. For an intermediate level network, the routing decisions must be made on the basis of the network numbers assigned to the organizations, some of which might be considered to have traffic conformant with federal use policies and some of which might not.

Although it is much more fine-grained than the current on-or-off rule of connected status, the use of policy-based routing based on networks is still a very coarse measure of control. Since the decision on acceptability is made at the network level, one has to assign a set of characteristics to all traffic emanating from or entering into a given network to make this strategy work. Strict application of such controls could prevent a commercial organization from legitimately sending research or scholarly data across the federal backbone: IBM needs to communicate with MCI and MERIT about NSFNET, but other parts of IBM may need to communicate on commercial matters. Organizations with a variety of uses might have to artificially define several networks with which to associate different use policies.

The practical result is that in order to support desirable usage patterns, government-sponsored networks will sometimes have to depend upon self-policing by traffic sources rather than upon strict mechanical enforcement of acceptable use policies. Higher certainty on usage will have a cost in terms of limiting desirable access. An important project then underway in the IETF was developing a more general mechanism for policy-based routing that would allow control at the level of individual hosts and possibly even users, giving an end host or user the ability to select routes taking into consideration issues such as cost, performance and reliability of the transit networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Knowing that a network follows a sensible policy does not let you police what it carries. The best you can do at the network level is to refuse to carry traffic for a whole organisation, which stops some legitimate traffic along with the rest.

sections.title: DNS and Connectivity
sections.content:
The Internet Domain Name system is an essential part of the networking infrastructure. It establishes a global distributed database for mapping host names into IP addresses and for delivering electronic mail, and its efficient and reliable functioning is vital to nearly all Internet users.

Some DNS operations depend on the existence of a complete database at certain root servers, in particular at the Internet Registry located at the Defense Data Net Network Information Center at SRI International. The past policy has been to tie inclusion in this database to approval of Internet interconnection by a United States Government agency. This connected status restriction is no longer viable.

The memo argues that the DNS database is not the proper architectural level for enforcement of administrative access restrictions, for example controls over the announcement of networks in the routing protocols. The IAB therefore strongly endorses the following recommendation from the Federal Engineering Planning Group to the Federal Networking Council, to provide DNS service regardless of access control policies. That recommendation reads: "There has been a great deal of discussion about domain nameservers, the IN-ADDR domain, and connected status as the Internet has grown to include many more nations than just the United States. As we move to a more global Internet, it seems like it would be a good idea to re-evaluate some of the rules that have governed the naming and registration policies that exist. The naming and routing should be completely decoupled. In particular, it should be possible to register both a name/domain, as well as address servers within the IN-ADDR domain, independent of whether the client has connected status or not. This should be implemented immediately by the IR at the DDN-NIC. No U.S. Government sponsor should be required for domain name/address registration."
sections.plainLanguage: Whether you may be listed in the DNS is a question about names, and whether you may route is a question about routing. Keeping the two apart means a rule made for one does not accidentally block the other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says plainly that security issues are not addressed in it. It is a policy document about who assigns Internet identifiers and on what terms a network may be registered and listed, and it does not discuss the security of those arrangements or of the identifiers themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not go into security at all; it is about administrative policy.

viz.caption: The three actions the IAB recommended to the FNC

items.title: 1. Drop the flag
items.text: The Internet Registry should drop all reference to connected status in its databases and in its registration forms.

items.title: 2. Ask for a policy statement
items.text: Each applicant should give a brief statement of acceptable usage, access and transit policy for external traffic, gathered retrospectively for networks already registered and published on-line.

items.title: 3. Open the DNS
items.text: Any registered network should be able to be entered into the Domain Name Server database without regard to connected status.
